title: Analog Platforms
intro: Analog quantum devices run a Hamiltonian directly rather than a gate sequence, which suits reservoir computing: the reservoir only needs rich, repeatable dynamics, not programmable precision. This page surveys the platforms on which QRC has been demonstrated or proposed and what each offers and costs at the readout.

blocks.text: What an analog platform must provide

items: An input channel: a control parameter that can be set per step from $s_k$ (a local field, a detuning, a drive amplitude, a reset-and-prepare of some sites).
Rich, fixed dynamics between inputs: interactions that spread the input across the system; disorder or irregular geometry to avoid symmetries that would leave features redundant.
Dissipation or a reset path, for fading memory.
A readout that returns many features per run, and a repetition rate high enough for the shot budget.
Stability: the readout weights are trained on one day's dynamics and must still fit tomorrow's. Drift is the analog equivalent of gate error.

blocks.text: In solid- or liquid-state NMR the reservoir is the dipolar-coupled network of nuclear spins in a molecule or crystal, and the readout is the free-induction signal of a macroscopic ensemble. Because the signal is an ensemble average, one run gives expectation values directly, without single-shot repetitions, and weak continuous readout disturbs each spin negligibly. The limits are polarisation (at room temperature only a tiny excess of spins is aligned, so the useful signal is small) and control (all copies share one Hamiltonian; local addressing is limited). Negoro and coauthors (2018) used the controllable dynamics of a nuclear spin ensemble in a solid as a learning machine, an early experimental QRC, and NMR motivated the spatial-multiplexing proposal of Nakajima et al. (2019), in which many small, independent reservoirs (different molecules) are read together.

Neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays, excited to Rydberg states, realise an Ising-type Hamiltonian with a global (or locally patterned) drive $\Omega$, detunings $\Delta_i$ and van der Waals interactions $V_{ij}\propto 1/r_{ij}^6$:

blocks.tex: H = \frac{\Omega}{2}\sum_i X_i - \sum_i \Delta_i\, n_i + \sum_{i<j}V_{ij}\, n_i n_j, \qquad n_i = \frac{1 - Z_i}{2}

blocks.text: Inputs can be encoded in local detunings or in the drive, the geometry fixes the couplings, and the readout is a fluorescence image giving the full bitstring per shot, so all one- and two-body correlators $\langle Z_i\rangle$, $\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle$ come from the same shots. Bravo, Najafi, Gao and Yelin (2022) proposed and analysed QRC on Rydberg arrays. Kornjača and coauthors (2024) ran quantum reservoir learning on an analog neutral-atom computer with up to 108 qubits, using measured correlators over several evolution times as features for binary and multi-class classification and time-series prediction, the largest QRC demonstration reported at the time.

Because each experimental shot reloads and rearranges the atom array, repetition rates are low (of order a few shots per second on current machines, against kHz rates for superconducting circuits), so analog atom reservoirs favour tasks without long recurrence (single-input or short-window processing, closer to a quantum extreme learning machine, see Quantum Extreme Learning Machines (#/qrc/models/quantum-extreme-learning-machines)) and readouts that extract many correlators per shot.

A single nonlinear oscillator already has a large Hilbert space. Govia and coauthors (2021) simulated one Kerr-nonlinear mode (natural in superconducting circuits), $H = K a^{\dagger}a\,a^{\dagger}a + \alpha u(t)(a + a^{\dagger})$, driven linearly by the input $u(t)$, damped by photon loss (which gives fading memory), and read through the expectation of one quadrature $\langle X\rangle$ sampled in time. On a signal-processing task (estimating the phase of a sine wave) it outperformed classical nonlinear-oscillator reservoirs, and the authors traced the improvement to the nonlinearity of quantum measurement. In optics, Gaussian continuous-variable reservoirs (Nokkala et al. 2021) are networks of linearly coupled harmonic modes (for example linear optical systems) whose inputs are encoded into Gaussian states, with squeezed-vacuum encoding giving the best performance; they are efficiently simulable classically, but they show how the encoding and the choice of measured observables set the reservoir's nonlinearity. See Continuous-Variable Reservoirs (#/qrc/models/continuous-variable-reservoirs).

Ghosh and coauthors (2019) proposed quantum reservoir processing, a different use of a reservoir: the input is itself a quantum state (an optical field incident on the reservoir) rather than a classical time series. Their reservoir is a 2D lattice of fermionic sites with random hopping, incoherently pumped and decaying, read through the site occupation numbers; trained linear readouts recognise entangled input states and estimate nonlinear functions of the input state such as entropy, purity and logarithmic negativity from that one set of measurements. Candidate platforms they name include semiconductor quantum dots, superconducting qubits, arrays of strongly interacting photons, and exciton-polaritons in microcavities. Being driven-dissipative, such lattices supply the contraction naturally.

items: Superconducting circuits (gate-based or analog): fast (µs steps, kHz–tens of kHz repetition), single-shot bitstrings, mid-circuit measurement available; tens to hundreds of qubits; noise and drift are the main issues.
NMR ensembles: expectation values in one run, gentle readout; small polarisation, limited local control, few distinguishable spins.
Rydberg arrays: hundreds of atoms, full bitstring snapshots, flexible geometry; slow repetition, so shot budgets are tight.
Bosonic modes: large Hilbert space in one device, continuous measurements; Gaussian versions are classically simulable.
Driven-dissipative lattices (quantum dots, photonic or polariton arrays): naturally dissipative; aimed at processing quantum inputs.

blocks.title: Correlator features from snapshots
blocks.text: A Rydberg reservoir of $n = 100$ atoms is imaged at $V = 10$ evolution times per input. How many one- and two-body $Z$-correlator features does that give, and what does it imply for the training set size of an unregularised linear readout?
solution: An unregularised least-squares readout needs more training examples than features (here more than 50,500), each with its own shot budget; in practice you select or regularise features heavily.
blocks.answer: 5050 per time, 50,500 in total; more than 50,500 training samples without regularisation.

blocks.title: Interaction range
blocks.text: In a Rydberg array with $V_{ij}=C_6/r^6$, two atoms 5 µm apart interact with strength $V_0$. What is the interaction at 7.5 µm and at 10 µm, as fractions of $V_0$?
blocks.hint: Scale by the sixth power of the distance ratio.

blocks.title: Shots per hour
blocks.text: A neutral-atom device takes 3 shots per second. You need 1000 shots per input for 200 training inputs and 100 test inputs, processed QELM-style (no recurrence). How long does data taking take?
blocks.hint: Total shots divided by the shot rate.
